title: Balance Sheet Building Blocks in Action
description: Practice classifying assets, liabilities, and equity while analyzing real-world balance sheet scenarios.

interactions.prompt: A retail company reports: Cash $50K, Inventory $120K, Accounts Receivable $30K, Equipment $200K. Which insight stands out most about their asset composition?

options.text: Most assets are tied up in long-term equipment
Inventory is the largest current asset by far
Cash position is dangerously low
Accounts receivable suggests poor collections

interactions.prompt: The fundamental accounting equation states: Assets = Liabilities + ____.

options.text: Revenue
Shareholders' Equity
Net Income
Retained Earnings

interactions.prompt: Starbucks 2023 snapshot: Current Assets $6.3B, Current Liabilities $9.2B, Total Assets $29.4B, Total Liabilities $35.6B. What's the most critical signal here?

options.text: Total assets look healthy at $29.4B
Current liabilities exceed current assets—negative working capital
Total liabilities exceed total assets—negative equity
The company has too much cash on hand

interactions.prompt: You're CFO of a growing e-commerce startup. You can either use $500K cash to pay down short-term debt or invest in warehouse equipment. Current ratio is 0.9. What do you prioritize?

options.text: Pay down short-term debt to improve liquidity above 1.0
Invest in equipment to support future revenue growth
Split evenly—$250K to each priority
Hold the cash and negotiate extended payment terms instead

interactions.prompt: Rank these balance sheet items from MOST liquid to LEAST liquid, as a bank analyst would assess them.

options.text: Accounts Receivable (net 30 terms)
Cash and cash equivalents
Commercial real estate property
Finished goods inventory

interactions.prompt: Two companies seek your investment. Company A: $2M assets, $800K liabilities, strong equity. Company B: $10M assets, $8.5M liabilities, higher revenue. Which balance sheet profile do you prefer?

options.text: Company A—60% equity ratio signals financial stability
Company B—larger asset base means more growth potential
Company B—high leverage can amplify shareholder returns
Need income statement data before any decision

interactions.prompt: The supplier just went bankrupt. $180K of your inventory was on consignment and must be returned. How does this impact your balance sheet?

options.text: Assets decrease by $180K, liabilities decrease by $180K
Assets decrease by $180K, equity decreases by $180K
Only liabilities change—you no longer owe the supplier
No balance sheet impact—consignment is off-balance-sheet

interactions.priorContext: You previously analyzed a retail company with $120K in inventory. Now assume $180K of additional consignment inventory was recorded as both an asset and a liability, and the consigning supplier has gone bankrupt, requiring return of those goods.

interactions.prompt: As a credit analyst, rank these warning signs on a balance sheet from MOST concerning to LEAST concerning for a mid-size manufacturer.

options.text: Current ratio dropped from 2.1 to 0.8 in one year
Goodwill represents 15% of total assets
Negative shareholders' equity on the balance sheet
Accounts payable increased 20% year-over-year
